extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Popular Science Monthly; educated lay audience interested in natural history and physiology
extracted.subtask_description: Magazine feature articles (19th-century Popular Science Monthly) presenting natural-history observations (archer-fishes) and physiological/psychological classification (temperaments), mixing descriptive natural history, historical review, and medical commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hippocratic temperament origins (four qualities)
rubrics_metrics.description: The four qualities of Hippocrates were believed to be the origin of the temperaments. In moisture and dryness, in heat and cold, not as conditions of existence but as entities in life, were found the materials that either singly or together formed the temperaments. They were combined thus: hot and moist produced blood, hence the sanguine temperaments; cold and moist caused phlegm or pituita, and from this the phlegmatic or lymphatic; hot and dry produced yellow bile, and gave us the sanguine or choleric; and cold and dry caused black bile, which predominating in the body resulted in the melancholic or bilious temperament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical/humoral taxonomy: use the four elemental qualities (heat/cold, moisture/dryness) to classify temperaments. The text notes this is an old classification that persisted long despite scientific critique; Haller (1757) placed phenomena on a physiological basis but retained the nomenclature. Use cautiously as a historical framework rather than modern physiology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanguine temperament (physical, mental, medical traits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanguine: mean height ~5'8.5" (male), face square, small head, firm angular jaw, slightly sloping forehead, prominent nose; chest large (~35"), spare fat, muscular, light/ florid complexion, light brown/auburn curly hair; mouth large, lower lip full, regular teeth. Mentally: vivid and active mental action, outward-looking vision, quick learning, ready tongue, bravery, quick anger but soon forgets. Medically: prone to acute inflammatory diseases (apoplexy, heart/blood-vessel diseases, haemorrhages, acute fevers, pneumonia, pleurisy); rapid recovery or rapid fatal result; crises/evacuations important—physician often should not interfere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanguine is characterized by vascular vigor and surface-minded mental style. Clinically, temperament is used prognostically (expect acute inflammatory patterns) and therapeutically (recognize natural 'crises' and avoid unnecessary interference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lymphatic (phlegmatic) temperament (physical, mental, medical traits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lymphatic: heavily framed, clumsy large-jointed limbs, awkward/slow movement, large head, unanimated thick-lipped pale face with listless expression; eyes blue/gray, abundant light hair; soft flabby flesh, small/slow muscles; late puberty, slow deliberate development. Mentally: passions move slowly, easily kept under control, conservative, logical, retentive, persistent, honorable, commonplace. Medically: weak in vital energy, short-lived, prone to structural changes (scrofula, phthisis, articular rheumatism) with marked hereditary force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lymphatic type denotes slow, retentive mental action and a one-sided abundant nutrition; relevant for prognosis and understanding hereditary/structural disease tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nervous temperament (physical and mental traits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nervous temperament: greater variety in physical signs; typically below average stature, small bones, lightly covered with flesh until middle life; large head, dark-brown/black hair not abundant; dark/sallow/pale skin with more pigmentation, hot dry firm cuticle; small compact muscles capable of sudden outlays of great strength but movements often irregular and poorly coordinated. Mentally: diversity in traits, imperfect motor coordination ('want of nervous coordination'), cerebro-central preoccupation (slow brain/spinal response).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nervous type shows high reactivity but poor coordination; described variably by different authors and sometimes introduced as an additional temperament (e.g., Gregory). Use as an interpretive category for individuals with high excitability and irregular motor/mental coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bilious / choleric / melancholic temperament (humoral origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the humoral schema: hot and dry produced yellow bile, giving the choleric; cold and dry caused black bile, resulting in the melancholic or bilious temperament. The term 'bilious' is retained in popular descriptions though some modern writers collapse it with 'nervous' or otherwise modify the schema.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bilious/choleric and melancholic categories are part of the classical fourfold humoral taxonomy; the text notes debates about retaining or merging this category in modern classifications—be attentive to differing nomenclature across authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperament versus idiosyncrasy (distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperament is built in a man, as bricks compose a well; his idiosyncrasy is developed according to the soil in which he is planted, the conditions under which he grows, and the tendency in him to vary. Temperament is a birth-right and a race-attribute (distributed by latitude/altitude), while idiosyncrasy belongs to the individual and is shaped by environment and will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying character/behavior, distinguish inherited temperament (stable, race/pandemic patterns) from idiosyncratic traits (individual, acquired, modifiable). This affects interpretation (e.g., epidemiological vs individual explanations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical analysis as empirical support for temperaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Table I — Ratio of Water, Albumen, and Red Blood-Globules in the Blood of Different Temperaments (figures as ratios to 1,000 parts of blood) — presented to show that sanguine, lymphatic, etc., differ in blood composition. The author states: 'This proves conclusively that temperaments have their origin deep and unchangeably fixed in the organic life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quantitative blood-composition differences (water, albumen, red globules) as biological evidence for temperament classification. The text presents this as empirical support for asserting physiological bases to temperaments; apply critically and consider sample/method limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical/practical importance of temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperaments have practical importance primarily in medicine: they inform disease susceptibility and clinical expectations (e.g., sanguine prone to acute inflammatory diseases; lymphatic to scrofula/phthisis). Temperament may inform treatment decisions, such as not interfering with natural 'crises' or evacuations in febrile disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat temperament as a prognostic and therapeutic consideration in clinical settings; identify temperament to anticipate disease forms and appropriate clinical management (with caution given historical roots of the schema).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for evaluating natural-history/behavioral claims (archer-fish example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of archer-fish shooting water to capture insects are reported from travelers and experiments (Hommel's pin-through-fly experiment), but other ichthyologists (Bleeker) found no confirmation and argue the celebrity rests on misapprehension and misattribution (hommel's observation applied to a different species).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate behavioral/natural-history claims by (a) seeking direct observation and experimental demonstration (e.g., captive experiments), (b) confirming species identity before generalizing behaviors across taxa, and (c) seeking corroboration from local observers/naturalists. Beware of accepting anecdote or misattributed observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomic/classification caution and alternative schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Various authors offer differing temperamental taxonomies: Dr. Gregory added a fifth 'nervous' temperament; Dr. Pritchard rejected Gregory's reforms and restored original terms; M. Michel Lévy classifies into three by excluding bilious; Dr. W. B. Powell proposed a 'human science' with ten compound temperaments. The text notes modern attempts to extend Hippocratic terms often fail to gain credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying temperament categories, be explicit about the taxonomy used and aware of alternative schemes. Historical and contemporary authors differ; prefer clarity and justify choice of classification rather than assuming universal acceptance.
